stories.title: Making architecture decisions arguable instead of announced
stories.s: Technology choices were announced rather than argued, so nobody outside the room could challenge them and debates reopened later.
stories.t: Make the reasoning behind each decision outlive the decision, without imposing heavy documentation.
stories.a: I set a standing practice: name the choice, name the closest shortlisted alternative, and link to where the why lives, in a small table.
stories.r: The practice carried across projects and became what new decisions arrive with, so decisions can be reviewed on their reasoning.

stories.title: High availability for a bot runtime that insisted on being in memory
stories.s: The chatbot platform's runtime holds conversation state in memory, so under high availability any pod restart dropped live conversations.
stories.t: Survive pod churn without rewriting the conversational runtime the product was built on.
stories.a: I checked alternative frameworks, found the same limit, and kept the runtime: sticky sessions, state persisted to Mongo, and Redis pub/sub to close duplicates.
stories.r: The platform ran multi-container with state surviving restarts, and the design documented its failure modes, including those the fix introduced.

stories.title: Wanting to build it in house and buying instead
stories.s: The bot platform needed web push notifications, and my instinct was to build it in house for future flexibility.
stories.t: Decide between building and buying, separating engineering reasons from personal preference.
stories.a: I wrote down what I wanted from in-house, weighed it against what the release needed, and recorded the preference and the decision against it.
stories.r: We shipped on the vendor, and the recorded trade-off made later customisation questions easy to answer.

stories.title: Taking a component out of the stack instead of adding one
stories.s: A messaging product ran Keycloak for identity, yet users, roles and organisations already lived in Dgraph, so every write landed twice.
stories.t: Remove the dual write and its compensating code, and get to one store of record.
stories.a: I checked which Keycloak features were used, found none beyond authentication, which NestJS covers, and wrote a decision record proposing its removal.
stories.r: The dependency and its rollback logic came out, leaving the backend with a single store of record.

stories.title: One model for everyone, or one per customer
stories.s: A document assistant for a fleet operator needed an architecture, and one model trained on every vessel's documents was the assumed default.
stories.t: Lay out the real trade-offs of cost, latency and access control instead of just picking one.
stories.a: I wrote both options out for client and team: one shared model versus one model per vessel, with pros, cons and the replica arithmetic.
stories.r: The partitioned design went forward, with the loss of cross-fleet questions accepted openly.

stories.title: A cache that remembered the failures
stories.s: On a regulatory document platform, generated documents came out wrong in ways that did not reproduce, and retries repeated the bad output.
stories.t: Find the true cause in a pipeline whose output reaches a client in a regulated industry.
stories.a: I traced it to a global result cache that also stored partial failed runs, then re-architected generation around per-step isolation with failure-aware cleanup.
stories.r: Failed runs stopped affecting later ones, a retry became a real retry, and the written root cause let the team review it.

stories.title: Tables that arrived in the client's document as raw markup
stories.s: Medical writing deliverables showed misplaced tables, detached titles, and sometimes raw markup visible as text in the client's document.
stories.t: Produce one root cause analysis for three separately reported bugs before anyone wrote a fix.
stories.a: I found three causes: raw XML mutation, incomplete model-emitted HTML, and context-blind placeholders. I moved tables to a structured contract with neighbour context.
stories.r: The whole class of defect went away, not just the three reported instances.

stories.title: Credentials in git history, and rotating keys was not enough
stories.s: Reviewing repositories before a host move, I found OAuth client secrets in git history, which ships to anyone who clones.
stories.t: Make the secrets unreachable, not merely invalid, before the repositories were pushed to their new home.
stories.a: I cloned bare mirrors, mapped each leaked value to a placeholder, rewrote history with filter-repo, pushed to the new remotes, and documented the exact procedure.
stories.r: The repositories moved with secrets removed from every commit, and another file with hardcoded credentials was flagged for cleanup.

stories.title: Holding back an accuracy number that would have looked great
stories.s: A large reported jump in search accuracy was circulating and was about to become a go-to-market claim.
stories.t: Check whether the gain was real, since repeated passing results seemed to be counted again across runs.
stories.a: I raised it plainly, then set a general standard: proposed improvements need a frequency table of failing cases and expected fix share.
stories.r: The inflated figure never reached a customer-facing claim, and benchmark results are now reviewed against a sheet before approval.

stories.title: A hiring process that does not depend on me being in the room
stories.s: Technical hiring for a research engineering role ran through me, a bottleneck and a single point of judgement.
stories.t: Build an interview panel that keeps the bar without depending on me.
stories.a: I proposed one lead and two shadows, shared candidate review beforehand, independent written feedback before discussion, and shadows who graduate into leads.
stories.r: The format became how the round runs, and the shadow-to-lead path grew the pool of interviewers.

stories.title: A one out of five, written so the candidate could act on it
stories.s: A research engineering candidate reached a working coding-round solution with AI assistance but could not explain why the Python worked.
stories.t: Score the round and write feedback that the candidate, recruiter and panel could all act on.
stories.a: I scored it low and wrote out the reasoning behind each mark, recommended not proceeding, said what to strengthen, and gave a reapplication window.
stories.r: The rejection was reviewable rather than a bare verdict, and the panel's differing views were visible to decision makers.

stories.title: Finding out what the cloud bill was actually for
stories.s: Cloud spend was climbing, and no single person could see which servers it went to because billing access was split.
stories.t: Establish the real footprint before deciding what to shut down.
stories.a: I scripted a sweep across cloud projects that listed every virtual machine with its project and state, then sequenced access, pruning and backups.
stories.r: Pruning followed the inventory instead of guesswork, and the sweep set the order of what to stop.

stories.title: Being asked to pull a date forward, and naming the real constraint
stories.s: Leadership wanted a cross-product integration delivered sooner because it strengthened the story with channel partners, which I agreed with.
stories.t: Show that the date was set by available engineering time, not technical complexity.
stories.a: I agreed with the goal, offered to make time visible through tracked tasks, and named three ways to buy time: delegation, clear ownership, hiring.
stories.r: The conversation moved from when it can be done to which trade-offs we accept, with the task breakdown as shared evidence.

stories.title: A port that turned out not to be a port
stories.s: Search training was to be ported from an older e-commerce AI codebase, and the files looked like a simple lift and shift.
stories.t: Scope the port properly before committing a sequence of stories others would plan around.
stories.a: I read the code itself: the crawler was tied to one storefront, so I called for a fresh generic crawl-and-chunk pipeline and resequenced.
stories.r: The order of work changed without changing the plan, and client-specific code stayed out of the generic package.

stories.title: Asking what onboarding was supposed to produce
stories.s: Two engineers were joining a document platform module covering audit logs, automatic mapping and server management.
stories.t: Give onboarding an intended outcome rather than just an activity.
stories.a: I asked the lead for the target outcome, how we would judge pace, and when production value was expected, and offered a reference checklist.
stories.r: Onboarding ran against a stated target and a first-value date, and the checklist was reused.

stories.title: Treating a tee-time booking as a reservation system
stories.s: A golf booking product planned a paid tier with automated slot booking, and the instinct was to build the feature first.
stories.t: Lead the product from architecture to launch, treating many users contending for one slot as the hard part.
stories.a: I framed it as a reservation system, put consistency over latency until payment clears and the slot is held, and deferred automated booking.
stories.r: The product launched on schedule to its user base, with the concurrency design in place before contention arrived.

stories.title: Overturning a hiring verdict by doing the review myself
stories.s: A senior engineering candidate had been assessed by a reviewer I trusted, and the recommendation was already written.
stories.t: Decide whether I agreed by reading the candidate's actual work rather than the review of it.
stories.a: I reviewed both pull requests, issue discussions and documents independently, then wrote my assessment point by point, differing on the algorithmic work.
stories.r: The decision changed on the merits, and the reviewer could see which points I accepted, setting the expectation that recommendations are examined.

stories.title: Taking services away instead of adding them
stories.s: Two pipelines had each been split into many microservices that shipped, failed and were debugged together, adding cost without independence.
stories.t: Make the case for consolidation on operational cost, with the boundary authors in the room.
stories.a: I wrote up the reasoning for a loosely coupled monolith, keeping only the seams with distinct scaling or failure characteristics and merging the rest.
stories.r: Fewer services to deploy, fewer cross-service failures to trace, and each remaining split could be defended individually.

stories.title: Reading the bill before optimising the model
stories.s: Model spend was climbing across products, and the instinct was to change models or shrink prompts without breaking the bill down.
stories.t: Cut cost through a mechanism we could explain, without switching to a cheaper model and losing quality.
stories.a: I reviewed usage per project so consumption was attributable, saw identical completions paid for repeatedly, implemented prompt-completion caching, and tracked the bill afterwards.
stories.r: Cost fell sharply with no change to models or outputs.
